source: GG14 ch8; KDT8 ch6; RangDale9 ch1, ch8; Sarkar p81-95

cards.front: Define pharmacovigilance and state its purpose.
cards.back: WHO (2002): the science and activities for detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing adverse effects or any other drug-related problem. The word joins Greek pharmakon (drug) and Latin vigilare (to keep watch). Its purpose is to reduce drug-related harm, inform doctors and regulators, support rational use, and guard against ineffective, substandard or counterfeit medicines.

cards.front: Define a signal, an adverse drug reaction and an adverse event.
cards.back: Signal: reported information on a possible causal link between an adverse event and a drug that was previously unknown or incompletely documented. ADR: a noxious, unintended effect at doses normally used in humans for prophylaxis, diagnosis or therapy. Adverse event: any untoward occurrence during treatment, not necessarily caused by the drug.

cards.front: Which landmark US laws were triggered by drug disasters?
cards.back: 1938 Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act after more than 100 deaths from sulfanilamide elixir made with diethylene glycol (pre-marketing safety testing). 1962 Kefauver-Harris amendment after thalidomide (proof of efficacy, reporting of serious adverse effects). 2007 FDA Amendments Act after rofecoxib (population surveillance, mandatory label changes, post-approval studies, REMS and public trial registration).

cards.front: Complete: drugs withdrawn or restricted after postmarketing surveillance
cards.text: Terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride and grepafloxacin: {{QT prolongation}} and torsades. Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine: {{cardiac valve}} abnormalities. Rofecoxib: {{myocardial infarction}} and stroke. Cerivastatin: fatal {{rhabdomyolysis}}. Lorcaserin: increased {{cancer}} risk. Thalidomide: {{phocomelia}}, though now used again under risk controls for multiple myeloma.

cards.front: Short note: Why premarketing trials cannot establish drug safety

points: Pivotal trials often involve only hundreds to a few thousand patients (median about 467): rare reactions are missed, e.g. nefazodone liver failure
Few patients with uncommon genetic variants (TPMT, HLA-B*5701, CYP2D6)
Median duration about 24 weeks; late effects missed (bisphosphonate jaw necrosis, atypical femoral fractures)
Children, pregnant women, the very old and patients with comorbidity are excluded
Mostly placebo-controlled; few active comparators
Surrogate endpoints can mislead: flecainide and encainide (CAST), rosiglitazone
High-dose rofecoxib approved for 5 days of acute pain was used long-term, increasing MI risk

cards.front: A patient develops jaundice in week 4 of a drug. Which four criteria decide if the drug is the cause?
cards.back: Temporal relationship (does onset fit the drug timing), previous knowledge (is the event a known effect), dechallenge (does it subside on stopping) and rechallenge (does it return on re-exposure; often unethical, so not done). Needed because the event may be due to the disease or other causes.

cards.front: Short note: Causality assessment of an adverse drug event

points: Event may arise from the drug, the disease or other causes; a clear yes/no is rarely possible
Temporal relationship
Previous knowledge
Dechallenge
Rechallenge (often unethical)
Definite
Probable
Possible
Doubtful
Naranjo algorithm for causality; modified Hartwig scale for severity
Regional PvPI centres do the causality analysis; reports reach the NCC through VigiFlow

cards.front: When are individual case reports most convincing for causality?
cards.back: When the event is otherwise rare, has few other risk factors, follows exposure closely in time (anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and the drug carries a large excess risk (e.g. rhabdomyolysis with cerivastatin, far higher per million prescriptions than other statins).

cards.front: How are signals detected in large spontaneous-report databases?
cards.back: Quantitative disproportionality methods compare how often a particular event is reported for a drug with how often it would be expected from the whole database; they need no exposure denominator but rest on unverifiable assumptions, so signals always need further evaluation.

cards.front: What is prescription-event monitoring (PEM)?
cards.back: A UK postmarketing method that follows cohorts of usually at least 10,000 patients on a new drug: questionnaires are sent to the prescribing general practitioners to record all significant events over about 6-12 months after starting the drug.

cards.front: Classify: methods of pharmacovigilance
cards.text: Pharmacovigilance uses {{spontaneous reporting}} and published case reports, {{prescription-event monitoring}}, computerised {{record linkage}}, observational {{cohort}} and case-control studies, {{targeted clinical investigations}} (PK, PD, genetic and interaction studies) and postmarketing {{clinical trials}}.

cards.front: What is the FDA Sentinel System?
cards.back: A distributed network of the FDA and more than 30 data partners covering over 100 million people. Each site analyses its own data under a common data model and reusable tools (e.g. propensity score matching) and returns results centrally, protecting privacy. It has evaluated signals such as olmesartan-associated sprue-like enteropathy and rotavirus vaccine intussusception, sometimes avoiding costly trials.

cards.front: Short note: Spontaneous ADR reporting

points: Voluntary reporting of suspected ADRs by health professionals (yellow card scheme in the UK, MedWatch/FAERS in the USA); mandatory for manufacturers
Cheap, covers all users from marketing onwards
Can detect rare and dramatic reactions quickly (thalidomide, fen-phen valvulopathy)
Massive under-reporting (only about 10% of ADRs reported; median under-reporting about 94%)
Denominator (number exposed) unknown, so incidence cannot be calculated
Reports often incomplete
Cannot detect small rises in common events such as MI
Reporting distorted by media, litigation and time on market

cards.front: Why can spontaneous reporting raise a signal but not give the incidence of a reaction?
cards.back: Only a fraction of ADRs is reported (about 10% voluntarily) and the number of patients exposed is unknown, so there is no denominator. Dramatic, early reactions get reported, so rare events can be spotted but not counted.

cards.front: Essay: Methods of postmarketing safety surveillance and how they complement each other

points: Premarketing trials are too small, short and selective to show rare or late harm
Spontaneous reports and case reports: cheap, whole population, rapid for rare dramatic events; under-reporting, no denominator
Quantitative signal detection on the report database needs no denominator; it relies only on spontaneous reports
Prescription-event monitoring: observational cohort of patients given a newly marketed drug
Record linkage, cohort and case-control studies; FDA Sentinel network of data partners
Targeted clinical investigations and postmarketing trials
Signals from reports are verified by controlled studies; regulators then act

cards.front: What are the goal and objectives of the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India?
cards.back: Goal: ensure that the benefits of medicines outweigh their risks for the Indian population. Objectives: a nationwide patient-safety reporting system; identify and analyse new signals; assess benefit-risk of marketed drugs; generate evidence on medicine safety; support regulatory decisions; communicate safety information; collaborate with and train other national centres; become a centre of excellence.

cards.front: Under PvPI, what should be reported and who may report (as given in Sarkar)?
cards.back: All suspected adverse events, including those from herbal, traditional or alternative remedies; especially all events with new drugs and drugs of current interest, all suspected interactions, and reactions causing death, life-threat, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly or needing intervention. Health care professionals (doctors, dentists, nurses, pharmacists) report; the source states lay reports are not accepted.

cards.front: Trace the flow of an ADR report in PvPI.
cards.back: The ADR monitoring centre (AMC, mostly medical colleges) collects the report, follows up for completeness and enters it into VigiFlow with source documents; causality is assessed (e.g. Naranjo algorithm, Hartwig severity scale); the National Coordination Centre at IPC Ghaziabad analyses the data and forwards it to the WHO Uppsala Monitoring Centre; CDSCO takes regulatory decisions and reports to DTAB.

cards.front: How is an individual case safety report (ICSR) assessed?
cards.back: For quality of documentation; coding of drugs (WHO Drug Dictionary based on ATC) and reactions (WHO-ART, MedDRA); relevance (new drug, i.e. within 4 years of first approval, unknown reaction not in the product information, or serious reaction); duplicate reports; and causality.

cards.front: Which drugs does Sarkar list as banned in India following PvPI data?
cards.back: Rosiglitazone, sibutramine, rimonabant, nimesulide in children under 12, cisapride, lorcaserin, phenylpropanolamine, gatifloxacin and tegaserod.

cards.front: How are drug names and adverse events coded when an ICSR is assessed?
cards.back: Drug names are registered in the WHO Drug Dictionary, which is based on the ATC classification. Adverse events are coded with WHO-ART or MedDRA.

cards.front: Short note: Evolution of pharmacovigilance in India

points: 1986: ADR monitoring system with 12 regional centres proposed
1989: six regional centres set up under the Drugs Controller
1997: India joined the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring (Uppsala Monitoring Centre)
National Pharmacovigilance Programme launched November 2004 with World Bank funding; suspended when funding ended in 2009
Launched 14 July 2010 with AIIMS New Delhi as National Coordination Centre
NCC moved to the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad on 15 April 2011
Run with CDSCO under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

cards.front: Short note: Materiovigilance Programme of India

points: Set up after serious device failures in Indian hospitals, such as incubator and phototherapy-unit fires and power-related deaths
Approved by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to make medical devices safer
Monitor adverse events of medical devices after they reach the market
Collect and analyse data systematically to guide evidence-based regulatory decisions
Monitor the benefit-risk profile and create awareness of adverse-event reporting among health professionals
Launched in 2015 by the DCGI
National Coordination Centre: Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission
National Collaborating Centre: SCTIMST, Thiruvananthapuram
CDSCO as national regulator; NHSRC as technical partner
Classes I (low risk), II (medium) and III (high); Class I self-certified by the manufacturer
Scope covers death, serious deterioration, serious injury and disability linked to devices

cards.front: Essay: Pharmacovigilance: need, methods and the programme in India

points: WHO 2002 definition; signal, ADR, adverse event
Limits of premarketing trials: size, duration, populations, comparators, surrogates
History: sulfanilamide elixir, thalidomide, rofecoxib
Spontaneous reporting
PEM, record linkage, cohort and case-control studies, Sentinel
Targeted investigations, postmarketing trials
Causality (Naranjo), severity (Hartwig), ICSR quality and coding
Label changes, boxed warnings, safety communications, REMS, withdrawal
PvPI 2010; NCC at IPC Ghaziabad; AMCs, VigiFlow, link with Uppsala Monitoring Centre
Under-reporting, data access, signal refinement, pharmacogenetics

cards.front: How often must a periodic safety update report (PSUR) be filed during post-marketing surveillance of a new drug?
cards.back: Every 6 months for the first 2 years, then yearly for the next 2 years. Post-marketing surveillance itself is mandatory.

cards.front: For a similar biologic, when can safety and efficacy trials be waived under the Indian guideline?
cards.back: Only when all of these hold: quality is comparable (physicochemical and in vitro); preclinical evaluation is comparable; clinical PK-PD, including PD markers and immunogenicity, is comparable; and a post-marketing risk management plan is provided. The waiver is not allowed if any one criterion is missing.

cards.front: What actions can a regulator take once pharmacovigilance data show a drug is unsafe?
cards.back: Change the label to restrict use or add warnings and precautions, or withdraw the drug; also circulate drug alerts, medical letters and advisories to doctors. Pharmacovigilance data feed these decisions.

cards.front: Short note: Risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS)

points: FDA-mandated measures, pre- or postmarketing, to manage serious drug risks
Medication guides, patient package inserts
Patient registries, documented safe-use conditions, laboratory testing
Communication to, education and certification of prescribers and pharmacies
Isotretinoin programme to prevent fetal exposure
About 60 drugs have REMS; effectiveness little evaluated

cards.front: How do regulators communicate new drug safety information, and how effective is it?
cards.back: Quarterly postings of potential signals, label changes, boxed (black-box) warnings, drug safety communications and public health alerts; also drug alerts and advisories sent to doctors. Evidence suggests communications are often ineffective: monitoring advice changes little, warnings affect new more than existing patients, work best when specific, repeated and with alternatives, and may cut prescribing in untargeted groups.

cards.front: What ethical problems arise in postmarketing safety trials?
cards.back: Randomising patients to a drug with a suspected serious harm and no expected extra benefit is hard to justify (e.g. rosiglitazone versus pioglitazone). An IOM review advised mandating such trials only when observational studies cannot answer a critical public health question, after reviewing all existing data, with heightened informed consent. Comparative studies early in a drug's life avoid the problem.

cards.front: Short note: Post-marketing surveillance (PMS)

points: Active surveillance of a drug after approval, under the conditions and population approved in the label
Often called phase IV by some authors, but not the same thing; it is an observational or non-interventional study
Pre-approval trials use selected, homogeneous patients for a limited time
Rare or late adverse effects appear only after wide use, so pharmacovigilance detects signals early
Prescription-event monitoring (UK model, cohorts of at least 10,000 patients)
Drug utilisation studies, case-control studies of ADRs, observational registries, adverse drug monitoring
PMS is mandatory for the marketing authorisation holder
Periodic safety update report (PSUR): every 6 months for the first 2 years, then yearly for the next 2 years
Drugs can be withdrawn or restricted if safety signals appear

cards.front: Short note: Risk-benefit evaluation of a medical product

points: Benefit-risk ratio: expected benefit weighed against harm
Harm: adverse effects, cost and inconvenience
Benefit: symptom relief, cure, fewer complications or deaths, better quality of life
Use the product only when benefit outweighs risk
Risk is a probability of harm, so the ratio cannot be measured exactly for each patient
Harm varies in nature, size and timing, from transient to lifelong
Therapeutic index is only a rough measure of safety margin
A clinical trial may begin only with a favourable risk-benefit ratio
Pre-marketing trials are often too small and too short to reveal rarer or later harms
Risk-benefit is reassessed continuously as adverse effects emerge
Tools: ADR reporting, label warnings, REMS and post-approval studies
Pioglitazone: bladder-cancer risk kept it off India's 2015 essential drug list
Same logic applies to medical devices under India's materiovigilance programme

cards.front: Define pharmacoeconomics and the ECHO model.
cards.back: The branch of health economics that measures and compares the costs and consequences of drug therapy (cost-benefit, cost-effectiveness, cost-minimisation, cost-utility and cost-of-illness analyses) to find best value for money. Drug decisions should balance Economic, Clinical and Humanistic Outcomes (ECHO). Regulators increasingly require economic analysis for licensing decisions.

cards.front: Classify: pharmacoeconomic analyses by how outcome is measured
cards.text: Cost-minimisation: outcomes proven {{equivalent}}, only costs compared. Cost-effectiveness: outcome in {{natural units}} (life-years gained, mmHg, cases cured). Cost-utility: outcome in {{QALYs}}. Cost-benefit: both costs and outcomes in {{money}}.

cards.front: When is cost-minimisation analysis appropriate?
cards.back: Only when two or more options are already proven equivalent in efficacy and safety (e.g. two equally effective antiulcer drugs, generics, me-too drugs or alternative regimens of one drug). Costs then compared should include acquisition, preparation, administration and storage. If equivalence is unproven, use cost-effectiveness analysis.

cards.front: List applications of pharmacoeconomics.
cards.back: Framing medication policy and formularies, selecting essential medicines and devices, allocating limited resources, guiding individual prescribing, reimbursement decisions by insurers and government, and prescription audit to cut cost burden and polypharmacy. Example: the large price gap between bevacizumab and ranibizumab for macular degeneration with similar outcomes.

cards.front: What is a DALY?
cards.back: One lost year of 'healthy' life; the unit counts early death and living with illness together.
refs: WEB WHO Disability-adjusted life year (DALY) metadata registry https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator-metadata-registry/imr-details/disability-adjusted-life-year-(daly)-estimates-for-0-4-year-olds

cards.front: How is a DALY built up?
cards.back: DALY = years of life lost (YLL) + years lived with disability (YLD).
refs: WEB WHO Disability-adjusted life year (DALY) metadata registry https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator-metadata-registry/imr-details/disability-adjusted-life-year-(daly)-estimates-for-0-4-year-olds

cards.front: What does YLL measure?
cards.back: Years lost to premature death in the population.
refs: WEB WHO Disability-adjusted life year (DALY) metadata registry https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator-metadata-registry/imr-details/disability-adjusted-life-year-(daly)-estimates-for-0-4-year-olds

cards.front: What does YLD measure?
cards.back: Years lost to disability in people living with a condition or its consequences.
refs: WEB WHO Disability-adjusted life year (DALY) metadata registry https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator-metadata-registry/imr-details/disability-adjusted-life-year-(daly)-estimates-for-0-4-year-olds

cards.front: What does a cost-of-illness study estimate?
cards.back: The economic burden of a condition, expressed as direct and indirect costs.
refs: WEB EuropePMC The economic burden of Borderline Personality Disorder: direct and indirect costs, and evidence from evaluations of interventions Front Psychiatry 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13662043

WEB EuropePMC Estimating direct and indirect costs of hospitalised typhoid fever in Indonesia: A multisite healthcare facility and community survey PLoS One 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13704798

cards.front: Name the two direct cost types in the Indonesian typhoid cost-of-illness study.
cards.back: Direct medical costs and direct non-medical costs.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Estimating direct and indirect costs of hospitalised typhoid fever in Indonesia: A multisite healthcare facility and community survey PLoS One 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13704798

cards.front: Which cost category covers productivity losses?
cards.back: Indirect costs.
refs: WEB EuropePMC The economic burden of Borderline Personality Disorder: direct and indirect costs, and evidence from evaluations of interventions Front Psychiatry 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13662043

cards.front: Which costing approach did the Indonesian typhoid study use?
cards.back: Incidence-based, patient-level bottom-up costing, using retrospective and prospective records.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Estimating direct and indirect costs of hospitalised typhoid fever in Indonesia: A multisite healthcare facility and community survey PLoS One 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13704798

cards.front: Why may cost-of-illness estimates be too low?
cards.back: Cost definitions are inconsistent, and components such as informal care and long-term impairment are often left out.
refs: WEB EuropePMC The economic burden of Borderline Personality Disorder: direct and indirect costs, and evidence from evaluations of interventions Front Psychiatry 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13662043

cards.front: Whose productivity losses are counted in BPD cost evidence?
cards.back: Those of individuals with the condition and of their family members.
refs: WEB EuropePMC The economic burden of Borderline Personality Disorder: direct and indirect costs, and evidence from evaluations of interventions Front Psychiatry 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13662043

cards.front: Short note: Cost-benefit analysis

points: Costs and benefits (costs averted, productivity gained, valued health gains) both converted to money at present value
Benefit-to-cost ratio = PV of benefits / PV of costs; net benefit = benefits minus costs
Ratio above 1: worthwhile; equal to 1: break-even; below 1: not economically beneficial
Allows comparison of programmes whose costs and benefits occur at different times
Putting a money value on health is controversial; avoid if benefits cannot be monetised properly

cards.front: Short note: Cost-effectiveness analysis

points: Costs in money, outcomes in natural clinical units (life-years gained, cases cured, BP fall)
Total cost divided by outcome: cost per unit of outcome for one option
Extra cost divided by extra effect when moving to the next-best alternative
Most cost-effective is not always cheapest: aims at cost optimisation
Supports formularies, essential medicine lists and policy

cards.front: What is cost-utility analysis and what is a QALY?
cards.back: CUA compares cost per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY), weighting survival by health-related quality of life on a utility scale from 1 (perfect health) to 0 (death); QALYs = time in a health state x its utility. It suits life-extending treatments with serious toxicity (cancer chemotherapy) and morbidity-reducing therapies (arthritis). Limits: no consensus on measuring utilities and difficulty comparing across populations.

cards.front: Short note: direct and indirect costs in cost-of-illness

points: Direct medical costs
Direct non-medical costs, recorded per patient
Productivity losses of patients and family members
Functional impairment generates indirect costs
Inconsistent cost definitions
Informal care and long-term impairment often omitted

refs: WEB EuropePMC The economic burden of Borderline Personality Disorder: direct and indirect costs, and evidence from evaluations of interventions Front Psychiatry 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13662043

WEB EuropePMC Estimating direct and indirect costs of hospitalised typhoid fever in Indonesia: A multisite healthcare facility and community survey PLoS One 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13704798

cards.front: Essay: Pharmacoeconomics: principles, methods and applications

points: Health economics applied to drugs; ECHO model
Drug acquisition, preparation, administration, storage; costs averted
Cost-minimisation
Cost-effectiveness (ACER, ICER)
Cost-utility (QALY)
Cost-benefit (B:C ratio, net benefit)
Humanistic measures: HRQOL, patient preference and satisfaction
Equivalent outcomes: CMA
Single natural outcome: CEA
Quality of life central: CUA
Monetisable benefits: CBA
Formulary and essential medicines, policy, reimbursement, prescribing
Valuing life in money, utility measurement

cards.front: Define pharmacoepidemiology.
cards.back: The study of drug effects at population level, including variability between individuals and populations under real-life conditions such as compliance. Regulators increasingly weigh it when licensing drugs. Observational pharmacoepidemiological studies are a key tool of postmarketing safety surveillance.

cards.front: What does a drug utilisation study investigate?
cards.back: Why and how drugs are prescribed, delivered, consumed and self-medicated, together with the non-clinical factors that drive drug use. Social pharmacology studies these reasons; clinical pharmacologists also run drug utilisation studies at tertiary care centres.

cards.front: Which study designs does Sarkar list for observing drug safety after marketing?
cards.back: Non-interventional (observational) studies, post-marketing surveillance, adverse drug monitoring, case-control studies of ADRs, drug utilisation studies and observational registries.

cards.front: Short note: Real-world data in pharmacoepidemiology

points: Insurance claims and electronic health records (large HMOs, Medicare, Medicaid)
Large, diverse, long-term populations reflecting usual practice
Quicker and cheaper than trials; can study rare and long-term effects and high-risk groups
Data not designed for research: coding inaccuracies, missing clinical details
Confounding by unmeasured differences (healthy-user effect)
Observational studies suggested HRT protects the heart; the Women's Health Initiative RCT showed no benefit and more breast cancer
Success: antipsychotics shown to about triple type 2 diabetes risk in children and young adults

cards.front: What is Mendelian randomisation and how did it predict a statin adverse effect?
cards.back: Grouping people by genetic variants that mimic a drug's action; since genes are fixed at conception, the comparison avoids biases of drug choice. Variants lowering HMG-CoA reductase activity mimic statins and predicted the higher diabetes risk with statins that clinical use took decades to reveal.

cards.front: What are pragmatic trials and their drawbacks?
cards.back: Large, simple, often open-label trials with remote enrolment and outcomes from health records, close to usual care. They suit relatively safe interventions. Poor adherence and uncontrolled co-therapy blur results: in ADAPTABLE (aspirin 81 vs 325 mg) many switched to the lower dose, so intention-to-treat showed no difference.

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacoepidemiology

points: Study of drug interactions, uses and side effects in a well-defined population
Studies how drug effects vary between individuals and between populations
Accounts for patient compliance and other factors that apply when drugs are used in practice
Voluntary reporting by health professionals
Prescription event monitoring
Observational cohort and case-control studies
Helps optimise drug use and drug safety monitoring
Regulators weigh its findings when deciding whether to license a drug

cards.front: Essay: Observational studies versus randomised trials for drug safety, with examples

points: Claims and health records: large, diverse, long-term, quick and cheap; can study rare and long-term effects
Weak: coding errors, missing detail, confounding (healthy-user effect)
HRT looked cardioprotective in observational data; Women's Health Initiative RCT showed no benefit and more breast cancer
Mendelian randomisation uses fixed genetic variants that mimic a drug (statin diabetes risk)
Pragmatic trials: large, simple, near usual care, but poor adherence blurs results (ADAPTABLE)
Use observational data to generate and refine signals; confirm with randomised or genetic designs where possible

cards.front: Which signal method needs no drug-use denominator?
cards.back: A quantitative signal-detection method. It relies only on the spontaneous adverse-event database and does not need the true volume of drug use (the denominator).

cards.front: Short note: Artificial intelligence in pharmacovigilance

points: Machine learning and natural language processing applied to large volumes of patient and report data
Aim: help detect possible safety signals in large volumes of data
Signal detection within spontaneous-report databases
Sentinel plans to add signal detection and AI to its observational work
Signal methods rest on assumptions that are hard to verify
Real-world data carry unmeasured confounding; a signal is not proof of causality
Signals nearly always need further evaluation before a causal conclusion or regulatory action

cards.front: What is AEFI and how does Sarkar group AEFIs?
cards.back: Adverse event following immunisation. Sarkar groups them into five categories: vaccine product-related reaction, vaccine quality defect-related reaction, immunisation error-related reaction, immunisation anxiety-related reaction and coincidental event. The grouping matters because immunisation-error reactions are preventable.

cards.front: Give one example of an immunisation error-related AEFI.
cards.back: Transmission of infection from a contaminated multidose vial. It is preventable, because the cause is poor handling, prescribing or administration.

cards.front: When is an AEFI classed as serious?
cards.back: When it causes death, needs hospitalisation, leaves persistent or significant disability or incapacity, or occurs as a cluster of two or more cases in one area. Serious cases get intensive investigation because risk acceptance for vaccines is low.

cards.front: Short note: Vaccine vigilance (AEFI surveillance) in India

points: Most of the paediatric population is immunised, so safety monitoring matters
AEFI surveillance began with the Universal Immunisation Programme in 1985
Five causal categories (product, quality defect, programme error, anxiety, coincidental)
Severity: common minor, severe, or serious (death, hospitalisation, disability, cluster)
Serious or severe AEFI: Case Reporting Format from the medical officer to the District Immunisation Officer within 24 hours
District verifies and sends the case to state and national levels; monthly reports cover minor AEFIs and a nil report is filed if none
Unexplained deaths after immunisation need causality assessment and a verbal autopsy form
Separates vaccine-related deaths from deaths due to other causes
Concomitant vaccines make causal attribution hard
Limited awareness of AEFI reporting in the private sector

cards.front: Define haemovigilance.
cards.back: A set of surveillance procedures covering the whole transfusion chain, from blood collection to follow-up of recipients. It collects information on undesirable effects of labile blood products and aims to prevent their recurrence. Its ultimate goal is to improve the safety of blood transfusion.

cards.front: What is the goal of haemovigilance?
cards.back: Continuous quality improvement of the transfusion chain through corrective and preventive action. It aims at donor and patient safety, appropriate transfusion and less wastage.

cards.front: What two scores grade a haemovigilance reaction?
cards.back: Severity (0 no sign to 4 death of the patient) and imputability (0 no relationship to 3 sure clinical and biological symptoms). Severity says how bad the reaction was; imputability says how sure the link to transfusion is.

cards.front: Short note: Haemovigilance and materiovigilance

points: Covers the transfusion chain; reports transfusion reactions, not only drug reactions
Immediate reactions: haemolysis, febrile non-haemolytic reaction, allergy, TRALI
Delayed reactions: haemolysis, GvHD, post-transfusion purpura, infection transmission, alloimmunisation, wrong component
Launched 10 December 2012 by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission with NIB, Noida as coordinating centre
Reports on the Transfusion Reaction Reporting Form, graded for severity and imputability
Monitors medical device-associated adverse events, such as death, serious injury or disability
Launched by DCGI on 6 July 2015; IPC is the national coordination centre; SCTIMST is the collaborating centre; CDSCO is the regulator
Both are quality-improvement and regulatory surveillance systems that feed CDSCO decisions

cards.front: Write the benefit-cost ratio formula and its decision rule.
cards.back: BCR = present value of benefits divided by present value of costs. A ratio above 1 means the programme's benefits outweigh its costs. Decision-makers prefer the alternative with the greatest benefit-cost ratio or net benefit.

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacoeconomic evaluation methods

points: Pharmacoeconomics applies economic methods to drug use: cost-benefit, cost-effectiveness, cost-minimisation, cost-of-illness and cost-utility analysis
Regulatory authorities increasingly require economic analysis, as well as evidence of individual benefit, when deciding on licensing
CBA: BCR above 1 means the programme is of value
CEA: ACER or ICER, cost per unit of clinical outcome
CUA: outcome measured in QALYs
Expressing health benefits in money is controversial, so CBA should not be used unless benefits can be expressed in money

cards.front: Nutrivigilance
cards.back: Monitoring of adverse effects from dietary supplements, functional foods and other nutraceuticals (also called nutravigilance). Why: in the US such products need no pre-market proof of safety or efficacy, so post-marketing adverse event reports are the main safety check.
refs: WEB PMC Nutrivigilance: the road less traveled 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10598719/

cards.front: Nutrivigilance in India: which national body takes adverse event reports?
cards.back: The Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI), coordinated by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, is the national ADR reporting route. A dedicated nutrivigilance reporting system is still lacking.

cards.front: Short note: Nutrivigilance

points: Systematic collection, analysis and evaluation of adverse effect reports linked to nutraceuticals
Also called nutravigilance
Dietary supplements
Nutrients
Herbal supplements
Animal-based supplements
Functional foods
Categories overlap; some products fit several
Many products claim health benefits without pre-market safety or efficacy proof (US)
Consumers depend on manufacturers or watchdogs for safety judgement
Manufacturers have a conflict of interest, so they should not be the main reporters
Consumer reporting is voluntary, so response bias is possible
US manufacturers must report only serious adverse events
Post-market safety data on supplements is limited

cards.front: Define biovigilance.
cards.back: Detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse events or problems with biological products (blood, cells, tissues, organs, vaccines). Why: it widens haemovigilance beyond blood.

cards.front: Short note: Biovigilance

points: Surveillance of adverse events and problems linked to biological products
Covers the full product chain from source to recipient
Blood and blood components
Cells, tissues and organs (including transplant products)
Vaccines and other biologicals
Haemovigilance covers transfusion of blood and blood components only
Biovigilance is the wider extension of the same model to other biological products
Biological products are complex and hard to characterise fully
Lot-level traceability lets an adverse event be linked back to the product and forward to recipients
A national biovigilance programme exists under the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission; programme details still to be verified from an approved source
